title: Link Shortener API
summary: Fix a link shortener that lets one alias overwrite another, add owner-only click statistics per day, then keep those statistics fast on hundreds of thousands of clicks.
overview:
You've joined the platform team that runs **TinyLink**, the company's internal link shortener. Someone pastes a long wiki or meeting URL, picks an alias such as `/handbook` (or lets the service generate a 6 character slug), and everyone who opens the short link is redirected. Links can expire, and every visit is counted.

It is a small Express 4 app split the usual way: `src/routes/` maps URLs to `src/controllers/`, which read the request and choose the status code; `src/services/link-service.js` holds the rules (aliases, expiry, ownership); `src/store/memory-store.js` stands in for the database, with every call asynchronous. Errors are classes in `src/errors.js` that `src/middleware/error-handler.js` turns into JSON. There is no real sign-in: the gateway puts the caller's id in an `X-User-Id` header.

Start with `README.md`, which documents every endpoint, status code and error shape: that document is the contract the tests check. Then read `src/app.js` and follow `POST /api/links` and `GET /:slug` from the router to the store. `node demo.js` starts the app on a free port and prints a short tour.

phases.title: Someone took over the handbook link
phases.instructions:
Two reports came in this week:

> **Ana (docs team):** *"Our onboarding page lives at `/handbook`. Yesterday it started sending people to a page I've never seen. The link history shows a new link was created with the alias `Handbook`, and my original one is gone. I thought aliases were unique."*

> **Security:** *"We can reproduce it: create a link with alias `Standup`, then create another with alias `standup` and a different URL. The API answers `201` both times and the first link now points at the second URL. Creating the exact same alias twice is rejected correctly."*

Find the cause and fix it. The expected behaviour is in `README.md`: aliases are case-insensitive, and an alias that is already taken in any letter case is `409` with `{"error": {"code": "alias_taken", ...}}`, leaving the existing link untouched. Keep every other status code and error shape as it is.

**Done when:** all tests in `tests/phase1.test.js` pass.
hints: Reproduce it with `node demo.js` or a quick test: create `Standup`, then `standup`, then fetch `/api/links/standup`. Which link do you get, and what did the second request return?

Following a link (`GET /STANDUP`) already works in any letter case, but creating one does not notice the clash. Compare how `findLink`, `saveLink` and `hasSlug` in `src/store/memory-store.js` build the key they look up.

`saveLink` stores each link under the lowercased slug, but `hasSlug` looks up the slug exactly as given, so `Handbook` is never found when `handbook` is stored. Make `hasSlug` use the same key as the other methods.
phases.answer:
**Root cause.** The store keys every link by the lowercased slug (`keyOf`), and `findLink` and `saveLink` use it, but `hasSlug` does `linkByKey.has(slug)` with the slug as the caller typed it. `create` asks `hasSlug(alias)` before saving, so `Handbook` is reported free while `handbook` is stored, and `saveLink` then writes to the same key and silently replaces the original link. Exact repeats work because the casing matches by accident.

**Fix.** In `src/store/memory-store.js`, `hasSlug` returns `linkByKey.has(keyOf(slug))`. One line; the service and controller are fine. (Alternatives such as lowercasing in the service also work but leave the store with an inconsistent contract; the key rule belongs in one place.)

**Verify.** `tests/phase1.test.js` has the case-variant tests (`HANDBOOK`, `standup`) that fail before the fix, and the exact-duplicate test that already passed. Also check that the original link still redirects to its first URL after the rejected request.

phases.title: Click statistics for link owners
phases.instructions:
Link owners want to know whether anyone uses their links. Add `GET /api/links/:slug/stats?from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD`. The route and controller already exist and call `getStats` in the link service, which currently throws `Not implemented` and returns a 500. The work is in the service, in `src/validation.js` (parsing the query), and where needed in the store, which already records every click with `recordClick` and returns them with `listClicks`.

**Rules** (see also the README):

- `from` and `to` are calendar days in **UTC**, both inclusive. `from` defaults to the day the link was created, `to` to today (`now()`, in UTC).
- Response `200`: `{"slug", "from", "to", "totalClicks", "daily": [{"date": "YYYY-MM-DD", "clicks": n}, ...]}`. `daily` has one entry for **every** day in the range, oldest first, with `0` for quiet days. `slug` is the link's stored slug (its original casing). `totalClicks` is the sum of `daily`.
- A click at `23:59:59.999Z` belongs to that day; one at `00:00:00.000Z` belongs to the next.
- **Only the owner** may read stats: anyone else gets `403` with `{"error": {"code": "forbidden", ...}}`. The caller's id is `X-User-Id`, which the router already turns into `req.userId`.
- Errors, checked in this order: `401` (no header, already handled), `404` for an unknown slug, `403` for a non-owner, then `422 validation_error` with `fields` naming **every** bad parameter at once:
  - a value that is not a real `YYYY-MM-DD` day (`2026-2-1`, `2026-02-30`, `yesterday`, an empty value, a repeated parameter such as `?from=a&from=b`) is an error on that field;
  - `from` after `to` is an error on `from`;
  - a range of more than 366 days is an error on `to` (exactly 366 days is fine).

**Done when:** the phase 1 and phase 2 tests pass.
hints: Keep the layers: parse and validate the query in `src/validation.js` (next to `parseCreateInput`, throwing the same `ValidationError`), and do the lookup, the ownership check and the counting in `getStats`. The controller already passes `req.query`.

Express gives you a string, or an array if the parameter is repeated. For a day, check the format with a regex, then make sure it really exists: a date such as 2026-02-30 rolls over into March when parsed, so compare `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` with the input. Do the 404 and 403 checks before you look at the query.

Get the link with `store.findLink`, compare `link.owner` with the caller, call `store.listClicks(link.slug)`, and bucket each click time into `new Date(ms).toISOString().slice(0, 10)`. Then walk the days from `from` to `to` (add 86,400,000 ms each time) so quiet days appear with `0`.
phases.answer:
**Approach.** `getStats` does the checks in the documented order: `findLink` (404), owner comparison (403), then `parseStatsQuery` (422, all fields at once). `parseStatsQuery` accepts only a string in `YYYY-MM-DD` form whose round trip through `Date` gives the same text (rejecting `2026-02-30`), applies the defaults (creation day, today in UTC), then rejects `from > to` on `from` and ranges over 366 days on `to`.

The straightforward counting is: load the link's click times with `listClicks`, keep those in `[fromMs, toMs + 86,400,000)`, bucket them into a `Map` keyed by their UTC day, then walk the days of the range and emit `{date, clicks}` with `0` for missing days. Total is the sum.

**Complexity.** O(C + D) per request, where C is the number of clicks the link has ever had and D is the number of days in the range (at most 366). Fine for a few thousand clicks; every request reads all of them.

**Watch for.** Using local time instead of UTC (`getDate`, `toLocaleDateString`), an exclusive end day (off by one at the boundary), forgetting empty days, and checking the query before ownership.

phases.title: A link that went viral
phases.instructions:
The all-hands link now has **200,000 clicks**, and the owner's dashboard polls the stats endpoint all day with different date ranges. Each request takes noticeably longer as the link gets more popular, and the server is spending most of its time re-reading the same click history.

Make the statistics scale: the cost of `GET /api/links/:slug/stats` should depend on the **length of the requested range** (at most 366 days), not on how many clicks the link has ever had. Behaviour, status codes and response shapes must not change.

Things the checks rely on:

- Clicks reach the store only through `store.recordClick(slug, atMs)`; the tests load their 200,000 clicks that way, then read them back only through the HTTP API.
- A click must show up in the stats immediately, including many redirects arriving at the same time.
- Slugs stay case-insensitive.

The test sends 50 stats requests with different ranges to a link with 200,000 clicks and has to finish well inside its time limit, and the answers must still match a brute-force count.

**Done when:** all three phases' tests pass.
hints: Where does the time go? Look at what `getStats` does with `listClicks` on every request: it copies and scans all the clicks just to count a few days of them.
Counting at read time is the problem. Do the counting once, when the click is written: keep a counter per link and per UTC day in the store, updated inside `recordClick`.

Add a store method such as `dailyClickCounts(slug, days)` that looks up each requested day in a `Map` (missing means `0`), and have `getStats` call it instead of `listClicks`. Keep the raw click list if you still want it; the stats must no longer touch it.
phases.answer:
**Why phase 2 breaks.** Each request copies all of a link's clicks (`listClicks`) and walks every one, converting timestamps to dates: O(C) work per request. With C = 200,000, every request is millions of operations plus a large array copy, so the 50-request test takes several times its limit.

**Optimization.** Precompute at write time. The store keeps, per link, a `Map` from the UTC day (`YYYY-MM-DD`) to the number of clicks, incremented inside `recordClick` (O(1) per click, one `toISOString` call). A new store method `dailyClickCounts(slug, days)` returns the counts for the requested days, and `getStats` builds the day list from the range and sums the counts: O(D) per request with D at most 366, independent of the number of clicks. Memory grows with the number of distinct days, not clicks.

**Correctness points.** The counter must be updated in the same synchronous step as the append, so parallel redirects cannot lose an update (JavaScript runs each `recordClick` body to completion). Keys use UTC days so boundaries match phase 2. Slug keys stay case-insensitive.

**Tradeoffs.** Pre-aggregation trades a little write cost and memory for fast reads; with a real database the same idea is a `daily_clicks(link_id, day, count)` table updated with an upsert, or a rollup job when exact real-time counts are not needed. Per-hour or per-referrer breakdowns would need more counters.

debrief: Why did an alias that differed only in letter case overwrite the existing link, while an exact repeat was rejected? How did you reproduce it, and why was the store the right place for the fix rather than the controller?

Walk through your stats endpoint: in what order do you check authentication, existence, ownership and the query, and why? How did you decide which UTC day a click belongs to, and what is the cost of one request?

Why did the phase 2 approach slow down as a link got more popular, and what did you precompute instead? What do you give up with per-day counters, and how did you check that an AI-suggested optimization still returned exactly the same numbers?
